Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively alternates between the two elements to maintain a steady, engaging pace across a narrative that spans several months. Summary and exposition are used to compress time (e.g., "For several months...", "In October...", "In April..."), describe the recurring nature of Daniel's dreams, and provide essential background information about his nine-year marriage to Rachel and his four-year relationship with Isabel. 

At the same time, the story relies on vivid, real-time scenes—complete with dialogue and action—for its most important emotional beats. Conversations with Isabel at the breakfast table, the discovery of the keys in the closet, the flashback of canoeing with Rachel, and the spring canoe trip with Isabel are all dramatized as scenes. This allows the reader to witness the characters' dynamics and emotional growth firsthand, while the summary smoothly bridges the gaps between these pivotal moments.
